extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, screenwriting teachers, and authors of screenwriting how-to books
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and guidance on how Aristotle’s Poetics should — and should not — be used in screenwriting theory and how‑to books. Focuses on correct attribution, interpretation, and limits of Aristotelian ideas when applied to modern screenwriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning–middle–end / three-act structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s identification of 'beginning, middle and end' is often invoked as the origin of three-act structure; authors frequently present it as a prescriptive rule that a drama must portray a protagonist’s problem and its solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify that Aristotle described beginning/middle/end descriptively for tragedy and used selectivity in what portion of life is told; do not simplistically equate this with modern prescriptive three-act, problem-solution models. Anti-patterns: claiming Aristotle demands a protagonist’s life-change arc or that every story must be a problem-solution narrative (examples: Richard Krevolin, Lew Hunter paraphrases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis — definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s idea of catharsis is often invoked as the emotional 'purifying' effect that should occur in the third act, but Aristotle himself mentions catharsis only fleetingly and does not adequately define it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-defining catharsis or using a single translator’s explanation as definitive (example: Hunter relying on S.H. Butcher). Treat catharsis as a contested and ambiguously defined Aristotelian term; support any claims about it with careful scholarship rather than rhetorical appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude = theme (misidentification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle describes tragedy as an imitation of an action that is 'serious, complete and of a certain magnitude.' Some modern writers equate 'magnitude' with the unifying idea or theme of a screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'magnitude' likely refers to the importance/worthiness of the subject and appropriate length, not directly to modern notions of theme. Avoid leaping from Aristotle’s 'magnitude' to claiming he established today's concept of theme without scholarly support (example: Linda Cowgill's extrapolation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action versus character (priority and relationship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle privileges action over character (e.g., 'life consists in action'), a point variously used or refuted by modern writers; some authors use Aristotle to assert 'action is character' while others claim Aristotle supports character-centered storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the nuance: Aristotle foregrounds action but acknowledges character’s role; do not misread him as denying character’s importance. Anti-patterns: using a single sentence out of context to assert a wholesale theory (examples: Syd Field's 'Action is character'; Lajos Egri's forceful rebuttal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity(s) of action, time, and place — correct attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Many screenwriting texts attribute the three unities (action, time, place) to Aristotle; in fact only the unity of action is decisively credited to him, and his comment about unity of time is qualified ('a single revolution of the sun, or but slightly to exceed this limit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assert that Aristotle mandated strict unities of time and place; note that strict three-unity rules became solidified only in the Renaissance. Anti-patterns: claiming a two-hour play must cover only two hours of life (example: Syd Field).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity of plot (portion of life told)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle praises selectivity in epic/poetry (e.g., Homer) — telling a portion of a life rather than the whole — so 'beginning' should not be read as literally starting at conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying Aristotle, emphasize selective depiction of incidents rather than literal full-life chronologies. Anti-patterns: interpreting 'beginning' to mean starting at a character’s birth/conception (example: Lajos Egri’s literal critique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting Aristotle’s genre/types (four kinds of tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle lists types (translations vary), but modern reinterpretations (e.g., McKee’s 'Simple Fortunate'/'Complex Fortunate') sometimes invent polarities or categories not present in the Poetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with genre labels derived from translations — consult the original context and multiple translations. Avoid creating new taxonomies (like 'fortunate' genres) that Aristotle did not articulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish tragedy-specific claims from general storytelling rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s Poetics treats drama in the context of Greek tragedy; many modern writers generalize tragedy-specific observations to all forms of drama and film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Aristotelian claims as originating in tragic theory and test their applicability before applying them wholesale to comedy, commercial Hollywood scripts, or non-tragic genres. Example anti-pattern: claiming Greek-tragedy aims (pity and terror) equate to modern screenwriting goals like problem-solving and moral redemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate quotation and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors sometimes misquote or attribute statements to Aristotle that do not appear in the Poetics (example: Hunter’s quoted line about 'what the hero is trying to get' not found in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify quotes against reliable translations and provide proper notes/bibliography. Anti-pattern: displaying Aristotle’s name to lend authority without accurate citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Aristotle to legitimize modern technique (rhetorical invocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: References to Aristotle in many how-to texts have a self-conscious quality, often used to legitimize a teacher’s own methods rather than to reflect Aristotle’s actual positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid invoking Aristotle merely as rhetorical authority; ensure the Aristotelian claim genuinely supports the technique and is accurately represented. Example: authors pulling selective phrases from Poetics to back up preexisting prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult multiple translations and scholarly commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations of the Poetics differ (Butcher, Cooper, Halliwell, McLeish), and no translation is perfect; relying on a single translation can lead to misinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read multiple translations and secondary scholarship together before claiming what Aristotle 'meant.' The article recommends Butcher and McLeish as complementary reads and warns that newer popularizations can repeat earlier misreadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-simplifying Aristotle into a set of prescriptive 'rules' for screenwriting
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenwriting authorities often bend, twist, or misrepresent Aristotle into simple rules (e.g., a checklist of beginning-middle-end, unity-of-time-as-two-hours, strict catharsis formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Aristotle as a complex theorist whose observations should inform but not be turned into dogmatic, one-size-fits-all prescriptions. Anti-patterns: packaging Aristotelian claims as a handful of immutable rules to be memorized and applied mechanically (examples throughout the surveyed how-to books).
